questions.q: Name the institutional dialogue mechanism that serves as the apex forum for India-EU strategic engagement, and state its frequency.
questions.a: The India-EU Summit, held annually (though gaps occur), is the apex political dialogue mechanism. A wrong answer (e.g., "Joint Commission" or "Trade and Technology Council") reveals confusion between the political-strategic layer and sectoral working groups; the Summit is the only leader-level format that covers the full spectrum from foreign policy to trade.

questions.q: Explain why India declined to join RCEP in 2019 despite its deepening "Act East" partnership with ASEAN, and identify the specific economic concern that drove this decision.
questions.a: India opted out of RCEP primarily due to inadequate safeguards against import surges, especially from China (via ASEAN routing), which would have worsened India's trade deficit and hurt domestic manufacturing and dairy sectors. A wrong answer citing "political differences with ASEAN" or "US pressure" misses the core structural issue: the absence of an auto-trigger safeguard mechanism and rules of origin strict enough to prevent Chinese goods entering India duty-free through ASEAN partners.

questions.q: A crisis erupts at the LAC in Eastern Ladakh. India simultaneously deepens defense exercises with the Quad and continues importing S-400 systems from Russia. Analyze how this dual-track behavior reflects India's "multi-alignment" strategy rather than "non-alignment."
questions.a: Non-alignment implied equidistance and avoidance of bloc politics; multi-alignment means simultaneously deepening security cooperation with the US/Quad (to balance China) while preserving Russia as a defense supplier and Eurasian balancer. The student who calls this "contradiction" or "hedging" fails to see that India treats each relationship as an independent variable optimizing strategic autonomy — the S-400 provides air defense against China, while Quad provides maritime domain awareness; neither substitutes the other.

questions.q: Compare the role of "shared democratic values" in India-EU relations versus "historical trust" in India-Russia relations. Which provides a more durable foundation for strategic partnership in an era of value-based foreign policies? Justify.
questions.a: Shared democratic values (EU) create normative convergence on human rights, rule of law, and multilateralism but generate friction when the EU links trade to labor/environmental standards or criticizes India's domestic laws (CA Article 370, farm laws). Historical trust (Russia) delivers reliable defense transfers (lease of nuclear submarine, S-400) and UNSC veto support on Kashmir but erodes as Russia pivots to China and India diversifies toward Western platforms. Durability now depends on interest convergence (technology/energy for EU; defense/energy for Russia) more than either values or history alone. A student who picks one as "more durable" without contextualizing the shift to interest-based realism misses the central analytical shift in contemporary IR.

questions.q: Evaluate the statement: "India's China policy has shifted from 'panchsheel and cooperative engagement' (1988–2019) to 'competitive coexistence with red lines' (post-Galwan)." Identify three specific policy changes that evidence this shift.
questions.a: Three evidence points: (1) Legislative: Amendment to FDI policy (Press Note 3, 2020) mandating government approval for investments from land-border-sharing countries (targeting China). (2) Connectivity: Formal opposition to BRI/CPEC on sovereignty grounds (skipping BRI forums) vs earlier exploratory engagement. (3) Border infrastructure: Accelerated construction of 3,500+ km of roads and tunnels along LAC, and deployment of 50,000+ additional troops — moving from confidence-building measures (1993/1996 agreements) to deterrence by denial. A student listing only "trade ban on apps" or "diplomatic protests" misses the structural, institutional, and military dimensions of the shift.

questions.q: Draft a 150-word policy memo for the National Security Advisor proposing a new institutional mechanism to manage the "Russia-China-India triangle" given the Ukraine war and Russia's deepening dependence on China. Specify the mechanism's mandate, composition, and one concrete deliverable for Year 1.
questions.a: A strong answer proposes a "Trilateral Strategic Stability Dialogue" (India-Russia-China) at NSA/Deputy NSA level, meeting bi-annually, mandated to: (a) deconflict Eurasian security perceptions, (b) coordinate on Afghanistan/Central Asia counter-terrorism, (c) establish nuclear risk reduction measures. Composition: NSAs + military advisors + foreign ministry DG-level. Year 1 deliverable: A "Transparency and Confidence Building Measures" (TCBM) agreement on missile launch notifications in the Asian theater, modeled on India-Pakistan 2005 agreement but expanded to include hypersonic/dual-capable systems. Weak answers suggest reviving RIC Foreign Ministers' meetings (already exist, ineffective) or propose India as mediator in Ukraine (beyond mandate).

questions.q: Fill in the blank: India's relations with the EU, ASEAN, China, and Russia constitute a multi-vector foreign policy strategy where India engages with these four major poles of the emerging multipolar order through distinct frameworks: a strategic partnership with the EU based on shared democratic values and trade; a "Act East" policy with ASEAN focusing on economic integration and maritime security; a complex competitive-cooperative dynamic with China managing border disputes alongside ______ collaboration (BRICS, SCO); and a "special and privileged strategic partnership" with Russia rooted in defense, energy, and historical trust, now navigating new geopolitical constraints.

Fill in the blank: Imagine you are a foreign policy advisor briefing the Prime ______ before a quadrilateral summit week: Monday in Brussels (EU), Tuesday in Jakarta (ASEAN), Wednesday in Beijing (China), Friday in Moscow (Russia).

Fill in the blank: Finally, identify the "deal-breaker" in each relationship (EU: data protection/human rights; ASEAN: RCEP opt-out/connectivity gaps; China: LAC/LoC; Russia: CAATSA/S-______/Ukraine war) and how India hedges.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can compare and contrast the structural drivers, institutional mechanisms, and key friction points in India's bilateral relations with each of the four powers, and evaluate how these relationships collectively serve India's strategic autonomy in a multipolar world.
